title: Why Don't Duck Feet Freeze at 0°C? 🦆
description:
Why don't ducks' feet freeze on ice? A countercurrent heat exchange in their legs lets warm arterial blood hand its heat to cold blood returning from the feet, so mallards lose only about 5% of their body heat through their feet.

topic: Why don't ducks' feet freeze on ice?
script: Ducks stand barefoot on ice for hours, and their feet never freeze. Yours would. Why? A duck's body runs hot, around 41 degrees. If that warm blood rushed into its feet, the ice would suck the heat right out. So inside each leg, there's a trick. The artery carrying warm blood down runs tight against the veins coming back up. As they pass, the warm blood hands its heat to the cold blood heading home. Scientists call it countercurrent heat exchange. So the feet only get blood that's barely warm, just enough to dodge frostbite, and the heat goes back into the body. In one study, mallards at freezing lost only about 5 percent of their body heat through their feet. And duck feet are mostly bone and tendon, with hardly any soft tissue to freeze. Pretty genius, right? So would you swap feet with a duck, just for one winter?
key_facts: Ducks and many waterbirds use a counter-current heat exchange between leg arteries and veins (askanaturalist, WWT)
Warm arterial blood heading to the feet passes close to cold venous blood returning, warming it and leaving the feet just warm enough to avoid frostbite (askanaturalist)
Mallards lost only about 5% of their body heat through their feet at 0 C (askanaturalist, citing study)
Bird legs and feet are relatively free of soft tissue; foot muscles sit higher in the leg and work via long tendons (askanaturalist)
Bird body temperature is about 106 F / ~41 C (Audubon via Forest Preserve District of Will County)
